course.title: Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection
course.splitRationale: The source runs about 4,950 words of narration - roughly 38 minutes - across 43 slides, which its two section dividers would make into one 16-minute and one 22-minute package. Three packages instead. Section 1 is the source's own Section I, taken whole: the framework and the blood technique, at about 16 minutes. The source's Section II is split at a genuine seam in the learner's task - collecting each of the remaining specimen types (about 13 minutes), then everything that happens to a specimen once it has been collected (about 9 minutes). That second seam matters because the transport, documentation and waste rules apply to every specimen type equally, and teaching them inside the urine-and-sputum material buries them. Each package carries its own welcome, objectives, summary and results slide as this studio ships.
course.learningTimeNote: Indicative seat time to work through the module once, attentively: narration at 140 words per minute, plus 6s per panel the learner opens, plus per-question time for each knowledge check, plus a 10% allowance for pauses, replays and navigation. On-screen text is not counted separately because it is revealed in step with the narration that explains it.

smeQueries.issue: The yellow and red top vials are both described as biochemistry tubes, with no rule for choosing between them. Slide 13 reads 'YELLOW TOP - Serum separator tube (all biochemistry and microbiology)' and 'RED TOP - No Preservative - Biochemistry test', and the narration says yellow is used for 'most biochemistry tests' while red is 'used for biochemistry and serology tests'. A nurse holding a request for an LFT has two tubes that both claim the test, and the wrong choice is a rejected sample. Please state which tube your laboratory wants for routine biochemistry, and what the other one is reserved for.

Slide 17 contradicts itself on liver function tests. It lists 'LFT: 6 hrs Fasting' and then, two lines later, 'Hematology, Biochemistry, Renal function, Coagulation Profile, Serology: Any time of the day'. An LFT is a biochemistry test, so the slide tells the nurse both to fast the patient for six hours and that no fast is needed. Many laboratories do not require fasting for an LFT at all. Please confirm which applies in your hospital - a nurse following the wrong line will either fast a patient unnecessarily or send a sample that is rejected.

The black top vial for ESR appears in the list of vials on slide 13 but not in the order of draw on slide 11, which runs blood culture, blue, red or yellow, green, purple, grey. A nurse drawing an ESR alongside other tests has no guidance on where it goes in the sequence. Please tell us its position so it can be added to the order-of-draw teaching.

Two different transport windows are given for urine. Slide 23 says to send the specimen 'within 15-20 mins'; the transport table on slide 32 says urine C/S 'within 1 hour'. The storyboard teaches 15 to 20 minutes for a routine specimen and one hour as the outer limit for a culture, which is the reading that makes both true. Please confirm, or give a single figure.

Slide 27 instructs the patient 'not to brush teeth on next day morning' before a sputum collection. Several protocols ask the opposite - brushing without toothpaste, or simply rinsing - to reduce oral flora. The narration hedges with 'according to your protocol', and the storyboard has kept that hedge. Please state your actual instruction so it can be taught plainly.
Slide 29 gives the normal adult CSF volume as 140-170 mL. The figure usually quoted is 125-150 mL. Please confirm the range you want taught.

The speaker notes on slide 18 are truncated - they end mid-sentence at the word 'After'. We have completed the procedure from slide 19's narration, which covers the same steps. Please review the final step of the blood collection slide and confirm nothing was intended beyond documentation and transport.

Slides 18 and 19 both ask the nurse to 'cross check with seniors regarding cost of the blood investigation' and to 'make requisition properly and send for billing'. These are administrative steps specific to your hospital rather than clinical technique. They have been kept, in the preparation step. Please confirm they belong in a clinical module, or tell us to remove them.

Several slides carry text left over from the decks this one was cloned from. 'Indications of Sitz' appears on slide 6; 'myocardial infarction' appears inside the titles of slides 7 to 19; 'ture of Water' appears in slide 22's title; 'Role of Nurse in radiology department' appears on slide 31; and a text box reading 'Abnormal muscle function' appears on slides 22 to 31. All of it has been excluded. Please confirm none of it was intended content.

Slide 31 carries only two headings on screen - 'NASOPHARYNGEAL SWAB' and 'OROPHARYNGEAL SWAB' - with the entire technique for both in the speaker notes. We have built the on-screen content from that narration. Please review the resulting slide and confirm the technique as written, particularly the insertion direction for the nasopharyngeal swab.

slides.title: What is pathology?
slides.designRationale: One idea stated precisely. The source's definition runs together the academic discipline and the laboratory work a nurse actually meets, and separating them is what makes the rest of the module make sense.

terms.description: The branch of medical science that studies the causes and effects of disease and injury
The laboratory testing of blood, urine, stool, body fluids and tissue used for diagnosis and treatment
The physician who specialises in this field

props.alt: Laboratory scientist examining a specimen under a microscope

candidates.note: Laboratory photos - prefer a clinical rather than research setting

slides.title: What gets tested
slides.designRationale: Seven specimen types, each with its own collection technique later in the course. Icons so they read as a set the learner will meet one by one, with blood marked as the one they will take most often.

props.text: Pathology tests help prevent, diagnose, manage and monitor allergies, infections, chronic disease and cancer. The sample you take is the first step in all of that.

slides.title: The three phases of laboratory testing
slides.designRationale: Three phases in sequence, and the whole point of the slide is which one belongs to the nurse. A numbered track with the pre-analytical phase expanded, because every task in that phase is a task the source lists elsewhere as a nursing responsibility.

props.text: The three phases of laboratory testing

interaction.buildAs: slide layers on this slide, not separate slides

layers.label: Pre-analytical
lines: Patient preparation · correct collection · proper labelling · timely transport

layers.label: Analytical
lines: Processing and testing in the laboratory

layers.label: Post-analytical
lines: Reporting and interpretation of results

props.text: Errors can occur in any phase, but most occur in the pre-analytical one - which is the phase you own. Wrong timing or wrong technique produces a wrong result, a repeat test, and a delayed treatment.

slides.title: Patient identification
slides.designRationale: The single most consequential check in the whole module, and the one the source itself marks 'very important'. A definition slide rather than a bullet in a list, so the rule and the prohibition sit together and neither can be skimmed.

terms.description: Patient name · UHID or MRN number · date of birth
The laboratory request form and the patient's identification band

props.alt: Nurse checking a patient's identification wristband

props.text: Never collect a specimen without confirming identity. A misidentified sample produces a correct result attached to the wrong patient, which is more dangerous than no result at all.

slides.title: Standard precautions
slides.designRationale: Five precautions that apply to every collection in the course, placed before any technique is taught so they are the frame rather than an afterthought.

items.label: Wear gloves and PPE as needed

slides.title: The order of draw
slides.designRationale: Six tubes in a fixed sequence, and the sequence is the entire content - fill them in the wrong order and additive carries from one tube into the next. A numbered track makes the order unmissable, with each tube's purpose expanded behind it.

interaction.buildAs: slide layers on this slide, not separate slides

layers.label: 1 - Blood culture
lines: First, to maintain sterility and avoid contamination.

layers.label: 2 - Citrate, blue
lines: Sodium citrate. Coagulation - PT, INR, APTT. Fill to the exact marked level.

layers.label: 3 - Serum, red or yellow
lines: Plain, or clot activator and gel. Biochemistry, LFT, KFT, serology.

layers.label: 4 - Heparin, green
lines: Heparin. Electrolytes and special chemistry.

layers.label: 5 - EDTA, purple
lines: EDTA binds calcium to prevent clotting. CBC, haemoglobin, blood grouping.

layers.label: 6 - Fluoride, grey
lines: Sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate. Glucose - it prevents glycolysis.

embeddedStates.heading: What each tube is for
embeddedStates.designRationale: The expanded state of the order-of-draw track. Each panel carries the additive and the test, which is the pairing a nurse needs at the trolley, with the reasoning in the narration so no panel becomes a paragraph.

props.text: The order exists to stop additive from one tube carrying into the next. Drawing out of sequence changes the result without changing anything you can see.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: The source's own scenario, placed immediately after the track. It gives a realistic set of requests rather than asking for the sequence in the abstract, which is how the order is actually used.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: A nurse is collecting blood samples for a patient requiring the following investigations: Blood culture, PT/INR, Liver Function Test (LFT), Complete Blood Count (CBC), and Blood Glucose. To prevent contamination of additives, which sequence should the nurse follow?

options.text: Blood Culture → Blue → Red/Yellow → Purple → Gray
Red → Blue → Purple → Gray → Blood Culture
Purple → Red → Blue → Gray → Blood Culture

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Please try again.

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: The recommended order of draw prevents additive carryover between tubes. Blood cultures are collected first, followed by citrate (blue), serum (red/yellow), EDTA (purple) and fluoride (gray). No heparin test is requested here, so the green tube does not appear.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: The recommended order of draw prevents additive carryover between tubes. Blood cultures are collected first, followed by citrate (blue), serum (red/yellow), EDTA (purple) and fluoride (gray). No heparin test is requested here, so the green tube does not appear.

props.onSubmitWithNoSelection: show InvalidPrompt — do not fail silently

slides.title: The vials and what they are for
slides.designRationale: Colour against additive against test against whether to mix - four variables a nurse holds at the trolley, and the source wrote them as seven run-on lines. The mixing column matters because shaking the wrong tube haemolyses the sample.

props.text: The vials and what they are for

rows: Clot activator and gel - serum separator
Do not shake - allow to clot
Fill to the mark, then invert gently

props.alt: Rack of blood collection tubes showing the different coloured caps
props.searchTerms: blood collection tubes coloured caps rack vacutainer

candidates.note: Tube-rack photos - prefer one where every cap colour is distinguishable

props.text: Invert, never shake. Vigorous shaking haemolyses the sample and the laboratory will reject it.

slides.title: Why a specimen gets rejected
slides.designRationale: Seven reasons, every one of them preventable at the bedside. Icons so they read as a pre-send checklist rather than as a list of laboratory rules.

props.text: Every rejection means a second needle for the patient. Checking the label, the fill level and the container before you send costs seconds.

slides.title: What changes a result
slides.designRationale: Eight patient factors that alter a result without altering the technique. Given their own slide because the nurse's job here is to ask and to document rather than to do anything differently.

props.text: You cannot change most of these. You can ask about them and record them, which is what lets the result be interpreted correctly.

slides.title: Tests that need something extra
slides.designRationale: Five tests, each with a handling rule that nothing else in the course requires. A table pairs the test with the rule, where the source's indented list left the learner to work out which rule belonged to which test.

rows: Collect before antibiotics. Strict aseptic technique. Two separate sites.
Antibiotics suppress growth; two sites improve detection
Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values
The level rises quickly if the sample is not handled properly
A prolonged tourniquet falsely raises the lactate
A single value cannot show the rise and fall of cardiac injury

props.text: Blood cultures before antibiotics, every time. Once the first dose is in, the chance of growing the organism falls sharply and the patient may be treated blind.

slides.title: Fasting and timing
slides.designRationale: Test against requirement - the question a nurse is asked by a patient the night before, and the one that most often produces a wasted sample. A table is the only shape that answers it at a glance.

rows: Haematology, biochemistry, renal function, coagulation, serology
Any time of day, unless the physician specifies otherwise

props.text: A postprandial sugar taken at 90 minutes or 3 hours is not a PPBS. The timing is the test.

slides.title: Collecting a blood sample
slides.designRationale: The core procedure, as a numbered track. The order carries real safety - identification before articles, labelling and explanation before the needle - so the sequence stays visible while the detail is explored.

steps.label: Fill the vial and mix if required

interaction.buildAs: slide layers on this slide, not separate slides

layers.label: Check the order
lines: Verify the physician's advice and the investigations required. Complete the requisition and send for billing. Obtain consent or clearance where needed.

layers.label: Identify the patient
lines: At least two identifiers, matched to the request form and the wristband.

layers.label: Prepare articles
lines: Syringes or vacutainers, tourniquet, alcohol swabs, gloves, labels and the correct tubes. Check the vial with a senior if unsure.

layers.label: Label the sample
lines: Barcode or patient details, per hospital policy.

layers.label: Prepare the patient
lines: Explain the procedure to reduce anxiety and gain cooperation.

layers.label: Hand hygiene and gloves
lines: Then apply the tourniquet about two inches above the chosen vein.

layers.label: Clean and collect
lines: Clean with an alcohol swab and let it dry. Insert the needle and draw in the correct order.

layers.label: Fill and mix
lines: Do not open the vial cap - puncture it and let the vacuum draw. Check the blood reaches the mark. Invert gently; do not shake.

layers.label: Document and transport
lines: Lab register, billing card, nursing notes and patient file. Send with the requisition.

embeddedStates.heading: What each step requires
embeddedStates.designRationale: The expanded state of the collection track. The technique details that decide whether the laboratory can use the sample - tourniquet position, not opening the vacuum cap, the fill mark - live here rather than on the track itself.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: The source's own scenario, closing the section. Every distractor is a shortcut a busy nurse might take, which is what makes it worth asking.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: A nurse is preparing to collect a blood sample for a patient's coagulation profile (PT/INR). While checking the patient's identity, she notices that the UHID on the laboratory request form does not match the patient's wristband. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Proceed with blood collection and inform the laboratory later.
Ask the patient's relative to confirm the patient's identity.
Stop the procedure, verify the patient's identity using two identifiers, and resolve the discrepancy before collecting the specimen.
Collect the sample and relabel it after confirmation.

feedback.body: Please try again.

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Correct patient identification is the first and most critical step in specimen collection. Collection must not proceed until the discrepancy has been resolved, because a sample attached to the wrong patient causes diagnostic and treatment errors.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Correct patient identification is the first and most critical step in specimen collection. Collection must not proceed until the discrepancy has been resolved, because a sample attached to the wrong patient causes diagnostic and treatment errors.

slides.designRationale: Added. The module's central claim is that the result is decided before the sample reaches the bench, and a two-option check forces the learner to commit to it rather than nod along.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Added. Fasting is what the patient asks about the night before, and the error is specific - applying one test's rule to another. A match tests exactly that pairing.

slides.designRationale: Added. Technique errors travel in groups rather than singly, so a multi-select asks the learner to recognise several at once - which is how they appear when a sample comes back rejected.

slides.title: Section 1 in brief
slides.designRationale: A recap in the order taught, consolidating the framework and the blood technique before the other specimen types begin.

points: Pathology testing of blood, urine, stool, fluids and tissue is what diagnosis rests on.
Three phases - and most errors happen in the pre-analytical one, which is yours.
Two identifiers, matched to the form and the band, before any specimen.
Order of draw: culture, blue, red or yellow, green, purple, grey.
The cap colour names the additive, and the additive names the test.
FBS and LFT 6 hours, lipid profile 12 hours, PPBS exactly 2 hours after a meal.
Do not open a vacuum cap, fill to the mark, invert - never shake.

slides.title: The urine tests
slides.designRationale: Five urine tests that look alike on a request form and are collected completely differently. Named as a set first, so the learner knows which procedure they are about to need.

slides.title: Collecting a routine urine specimen
slides.designRationale: Seven steps, several of which happen the night before. A numbered track so the preparation that has to precede the collection is visible as part of the procedure rather than as advice.

steps.label: Inform the patient the previous night
Leave the container at the bedside
Explain perineal cleaning with soap and water

props.alt: Sterile screw-capped urine specimen container with a label
props.searchTerms: urine specimen container screw cap sterile

props.text: Midstream means the patient starts to void, discards the first portion, then collects. The first portion carries the contaminants the test is trying to avoid.

slides.title: Urine for culture and sensitivity
slides.designRationale: Two completely different techniques depending on whether the patient has a catheter, set side by side because choosing the wrong one produces a contaminated sample and an antibiotic the patient did not need.

columns.title: Patient can void
columns.body:
Sterile screw-capped container.
Same midstream clean-catch method as for a routine specimen.

columns.title: Patient has a Foley catheter
columns.body:
Clamp the tubing below the port for 20–30 minutes.
Clean the port with an alcohol swab.
Aspirate with a sterile syringe through the sampling port.

props.text: Never collect urine for culture from the drainage bag. Bag urine is colonised and will grow organisms that are not infecting the patient.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: The source's own question, placed straight after the comparison. Option A is the shortcut that is actually taken on busy wards, which is precisely why it is worth testing.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: A patient with an indwelling Foley catheter requires a urine sample for culture and sensitivity (C/S). What is the correct method of specimen collection?

options.text: Collect urine from the drainage bag.
Remove the catheter and collect the first urine.
Clamp the catheter, disinfect the sampling port, and collect urine using a sterile syringe.
Ask the patient to void around the catheter.

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Please try again.

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Urine for culture should never be collected from the drainage bag, because it is contaminated. Fresh urine is obtained aseptically from the sampling port after clamping the catheter.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Urine for culture should never be collected from the drainage bag, because it is contaminated. Fresh urine is obtained aseptically from the sampling port after clamping the catheter.

props.onSubmitWithNoSelection: show InvalidPrompt — do not fail silently

slides.title: The 24-hour urine collection
slides.designRationale: A collection that runs for a day across several shifts, where one missed void invalidates the whole thing. A numbered track, because the discard-and-start-the-clock step is the one everybody gets wrong.
slides.devNotes: Spot sodium and microalbumin are stat collections - any time, clean labelled container, sent promptly. Carried in the narration of this slide.

steps.label: Obtain the jar from the laboratory and label it
Ask the patient to void - discard this urine
Record that time: the 24 hours start here
Collect every void into the jar for 24 hours
At the same time next day, collect the final specimen
Close the jar and send it with the requisition

props.text: The first urine is discarded and the clock starts then. Including it - or missing a single void during the day - makes the whole 24-hour result wrong.

slides.title: Collecting sputum
slides.designRationale: Seven steps, and the whole procedure turns on one distinction the patient has to be taught - sputum from the chest, not saliva from the mouth. A numbered track with that distinction lifted into a warning.

steps.label: Inform the patient the previous night
Leave a sterile container at the bedside
Next morning, rinse the mouth with plain water

props.text: Saliva is not sputum. The sample should be thick and mucoid - watery saliva will be rejected or will grow mouth flora instead of the pathogen.

slides.title: Stool specimens
slides.designRationale: Three tests with three completely different rules, including drug holds that start a week before. A table pairs each test with its own instruction, where the source's single list made them look interchangeable.

rows: Stool for OPC - ova, parasite, cyst
Three samples on three different days
1–3 days between samples. To the laboratory within 2 hours
Stool for OBT - occult blood test
Stop NSAIDs - aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin - for 7 days. Stop iron for 3 days. Collect 3 days before or after menstruation

props.text: The occult blood drug holds are stopped only on medical advice. Seven days without aspirin is a clinical decision, not a laboratory one.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid
slides.designRationale: The one specimen in the course the nurse does not collect. Defined on its own slide so the division of responsibility - clinician collects, nurse prepares and monitors - is explicit before the articles and the aftercare are taught.

terms.description: Clear fluid in the subarachnoid space, surrounding the brain in the skull and the spinal cord in the spinal column
A trained clinician only, by lumbar puncture, under strict aseptic precautions

props.alt: Lumbar puncture tray set out with needles, syringes and specimen bottles
props.searchTerms: lumbar puncture tray sterile needles bottles

candidates.note: LP tray photos - prefer a laid-out sterile tray

props.text: Your part is preparation, positioning, asepsis, monitoring and immediate transport. The needle is not yours, but everything around it is.

slides.title: Articles to have ready
slides.designRationale: Five items the nurse assembles before the clinician arrives. Icons so the tray can be checked at a glance, which is how it is actually done.

props.text: Label the containers before the procedure starts. CSF is numbered in the order the bottles are filled, and that order is part of the result.

slides.title: Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs
slides.designRationale: Two techniques that sound similar and go to completely different places. The source slide carried only the two headings with the whole technique in narration, so the content is built here from the narration and set side by side - the direction of insertion is the part that is got wrong.

columns.title: Nasopharyngeal
columns.body:
Blow the nose; head tilted slightly back.
Insert the flexible swab parallel to the palate.
Straight back towards the ear, not upward.
Advance until resistance; rotate gently.
Leave a few seconds, then withdraw slowly.

columns.title: Oropharyngeal
columns.body:
Open wide and say 'Ahh'.
Tongue depressor if needed.
Rub both tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharynx.
Avoid the tongue, teeth and gums.

props.text: Directed upward instead of straight back, a nasopharyngeal swab is painful and samples the wrong place. Parallel to the palate, towards the ear.

slides.title: Section 2 in brief
slides.designRationale: A recap specimen by specimen, which is how a nurse will come back to this section - looking up one procedure at a time.

points: Routine urine: early morning, midstream clean catch, sent within 15–20 minutes.
Urine C/S: sterile container. From a Foley, clamp 20–30 min and aspirate from the port - never the bag.
24-hour urine: discard the first void, record the time, collect every void after it.
Sputum: early morning, rinse the mouth, cough from the chest - not saliva.
Stool OPC three days; OBT needs NSAIDs stopped 7 days and iron 3 days.
CSF is taken by a clinician; you prepare, position, monitor and send immediately.
Swabs: nasopharyngeal parallel to the palate; oropharyngeal avoiding tongue and teeth.

slides.title: Transport requirements
slides.designRationale: Specimen against requirement against reason. The source already had this as a table, correctly - the third column is added because a nurse who knows why CSF is not refrigerated will not refrigerate it at three in the morning.

rows: Delay reduces recovery of the organism
Some organisms do not survive cooling
Bacteria multiply in the container and distort the count
Overnight secretions give a more concentrated sample
Urine, water or menstrual blood will alter the result
On ice if delay is expected
Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values

props.alt: Specimen in a sealed biohazard transport bag with the requisition form

props.text: CSF is the exception that catches people out: immediate, and never refrigerated.

slides.title: Critical specimens
slides.designRationale: Six specimens where a delay changes a treatment decision rather than just a number. Given their own slide so the learner can recognise one on a tray and move it to the front of the queue.

props.text: These six do not wait for the next round. A delayed potassium or troponin postpones a decision that is being made now.

slides.title: What to document
slides.designRationale: Five fields, each one something the laboratory or the next nurse will need. Treated as a named set because documentation is checked off rather than written as prose.

props.text: Record it in the laboratory register, the nursing notes and the patient's file - all three. One entry in one place is not traceable.

slides.title: Complications by procedure
slides.designRationale: Three procedures with distinct complications, grouped so the learner knows what to watch for after each one rather than holding a single undifferentiated list.

rows: Correct technique and firm post-procedure pressure
Lying flat as protocol specifies, and close monitoring
Contamination - bacteria, vaginal secretions, stool, water
Clean catch technique and a sterile container

slides.title: What to teach the patient
slides.designRationale: Five teaching points, most of which the patient has to act on when no nurse is present. Their own slide, because a specimen collected at home or unsupervised is only as good as the instruction that preceded it.

slides.title: Quality control and infection prevention
slides.designRationale: Four habits that protect the sample and the handler at the same time. Grouped on one slide because they are performed together, in the same few seconds, at the end of every collection.

props.text: Double-checking the label is the last chance to catch an error that the laboratory cannot see and cannot correct.

slides.title: Biomedical waste segregation
slides.designRationale: Four colour-coded streams, where the colour is the whole instruction. Icons with the colour named in the label, because this is recalled visually at the bin rather than read.

props.text: A needle in the wrong bag injures whoever handles it next. Sharps go in the puncture-proof white container, at the point of use.

slides.title: Common laboratory abbreviations
slides.designRationale: Eight abbreviations the learner will read on request forms every day. A two-column table because this is a reference to be scanned rather than a concept to be understood.

slides.title: Errors to avoid
slides.designRationale: Six specific errors, every one of which appears somewhere earlier in the course as a rule. Collected here as a closing checklist, because this is the slide a nurse will screenshot.

items.label: Drawing above an IV infusion line

props.text: Never draw from a vein above a running infusion. The result will look like a real one and be diluted.

slides.title: Key points
slides.designRationale: The closing recap for the whole course, spanning all three sections rather than this one alone, because this is where the learner finishes.

points: Pathology investigations support accurate diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.
Most laboratory errors happen before the sample reaches the bench.
Two identifiers, the right container, the right order of draw, the right fill.
Follow the test-specific rules: fasting, timing, asepsis, drug holds.
Blood culture and CSF go immediately; CSF is never refrigerated.
Document time, specimen, collector, preparation and anything unusual.
Teach the patient, segregate the waste, and check the label twice.
